claim: Throughout development, the brain transits from early highly synchronous activity patterns to a mature state with sparse and decorrelated neural activity.
source: Throughout development, the brain transits from early highly synchronous activity patterns to a mature state with sparse and decorrelated neural activity, yet the mechanisms underlying this process are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle of brain development.

claim: Decorrelated and sparse activity allows for more efficient storage, retrieval, and processing of information.
source: The developmental transition has important functional consequences, as the latter state is thought to allow for more efficient storage, retrieval, and processing of information.
evidence: This functional consequence is stated in the abstract.

claim: In the mouse medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), neural activity during the first two postnatal weeks decorrelates following specific spatial patterns.
source: Here, we show that, in the mouse medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), neural activity during the first two postnatal weeks decorrelates following specific spatial patterns.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: The decorrelation of neural activity in the mouse mPFC is accompanied by a concomitant tilting of excitation-inhibition (E-I) ratio toward inhibition.
source: This process is accompanied by a concomitant tilting of excitation-inhibition (E-I) ratio toward inhibition.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: A relative increase of inhibition drives the decorrelation of neural activity.
source: Using optogenetic manipulations and neural network modeling, we show that the two phenomena are mechanistically linked, and that a relative increase of inhibition drives the decorrelation of neural activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through optogenetic experiments and computational modeling.

claim: In mice mimicking the etiology of neurodevelopmental disorders, subtle alterations in E-I ratio are associated with specific impairments in the correlational structure of spike trains.
source: Accordingly, in mice mimicking the etiology of neurodevelopmental disorders, subtle alterations in E-I ratio are associated with specific impairments in the correlational structure of spike trains.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of data from GE mice, a model of neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: An analogous developmental transition in E-I ratio takes place in the human brain.
source: Finally, capitalizing on EEG data from newborn babies, we show that an analogous developmental transition takes place also in the human brain.
evidence: This is based on analysis of two EEG datasets from human newborns.

claim: Changes in E-I ratio control the (de)correlation of neural activity.
source: Thus, changes in E-I ratio control the (de)correlation of neural activity and, by these means, its developmental imbalance might contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined experimental and modeling results.

claim: Developmental imbalance in E-I ratio might contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Thus, changes in E-I ratio control the (de)correlation of neural activity and, by these means, its developmental imbalance might contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in disease models.

claim: Neural activity in the developing brain is characterized by discontinuity.
source: Neural activity in the developing brain has several unique traits, such as discontinuity (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021), extremely low firing rates (Shen and Colonnese, 2016), a loose temporal coordination of excitation and inhibition (Dorrn et al., 2010), and weak modulation by behavioral state (Cirelli and Tononi, 2015; Chini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity in the developing brain is characterized by extremely low firing rates.
source: Neural activity in the developing brain has several unique traits, such as discontinuity (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021), extremely low firing rates (Shen and Colonnese, 2016), a loose temporal coordination of excitation and inhibition (Dorrn et al., 2010), and weak modulation by behavioral state (Cirelli and Tononi, 2015; Chini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity in the developing brain is characterized by loose temporal coordination of excitation and inhibition.
source: Neural activity in the developing brain has several unique traits, such as discontinuity (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021), extremely low firing rates (Shen and Colonnese, 2016), a loose temporal coordination of excitation and inhibition (Dorrn et al., 2010), and weak modulation by behavioral state (Cirelli and Tononi, 2015; Chini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity in the developing brain is characterized by weak modulation by behavioral state.
source: Neural activity in the developing brain has several unique traits, such as discontinuity (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021), extremely low firing rates (Shen and Colonnese, 2016), a loose temporal coordination of excitation and inhibition (Dorrn et al., 2010), and weak modulation by behavioral state (Cirelli and Tononi, 2015; Chini et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Patterns of early brain activity have been described in humans.
source: These patterns of early activity have been described in humans (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006) as well as in disparate model organisms ranging from fish (Avitan et al., 2017) to flies (Akin et al., 2019), and from rodents (Khazipov et al., 2004) to brain organoids (Trujillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Patterns of early brain activity have been described in fish.
source: These patterns of early activity have been described in humans (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006) as well as in disparate model organisms ranging from fish (Avitan et al., 2017) to flies (Akin et al., 2019), and from rodents (Khazipov et al., 2004) to brain organoids (Trujillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Patterns of early brain activity have been described in flies.
source: These patterns of early activity have been described in humans (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006) as well as in disparate model organisms ranging from fish (Avitan et al., 2017) to flies (Akin et al., 2019), and from rodents (Khazipov et al., 2004) to brain organoids (Trujillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Patterns of early brain activity have been described in rodents.
source: These patterns of early activity have been described in humans (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006) as well as in disparate model organisms ranging from fish (Avitan et al., 2017) to flies (Akin et al., 2019), and from rodents (Khazipov et al., 2004) to brain organoids (Trujillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Patterns of early brain activity have been described in brain organoids.
source: These patterns of early activity have been described in humans (Vanhatalo and Kaila, 2006) as well as in disparate model organisms ranging from fish (Avitan et al., 2017) to flies (Akin et al., 2019), and from rodents (Khazipov et al., 2004) to brain organoids (Trujillo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: As brain networks mature, oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency.
source: Oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency (Bitzenhofer et al., 2020), oscillation patterns become more complex (Trujillo et al., 2019), the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases (Zhang et al., 2011), excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale (Dorrn et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018), and brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: As brain networks mature, oscillation patterns become more complex.
source: Oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency (Bitzenhofer et al., 2020), oscillation patterns become more complex (Trujillo et al., 2019), the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases (Zhang et al., 2011), excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale (Dorrn et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018), and brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: As brain networks mature, the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases.
source: Oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency (Bitzenhofer et al., 2020), oscillation patterns become more complex (Trujillo et al., 2019), the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases (Zhang et al., 2011), excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale (Dorrn et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018), and brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: As brain networks mature, excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale.
source: Oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency (Bitzenhofer et al., 2020), oscillation patterns become more complex (Trujillo et al., 2019), the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases (Zhang et al., 2011), excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale (Dorrn et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018), and brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: As brain networks mature, brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies.
source: Oscillatory events become more rhythmic, increasing their amplitude and average frequency (Bitzenhofer et al., 2020), oscillation patterns become more complex (Trujillo et al., 2019), the ratio of excitatory and inhibitory conductances (E-I ratio) decreases (Zhang et al., 2011), excitation and inhibition tighten on a temporal scale (Dorrn et al., 2010; Moore et al., 2018), and brain activity decorrelates and sparsifies (Golshani et al., 2009; Rochefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relationship between decorrelation and E-I ratio has been the subject of extensive experimental and theoretical work in the adult brain.
source: The relationship between decorrelation and E-I ratio has been the subject of extensive experimental and theoretical work in the adult brain (Zhou and Yu, 2014; Yu et al., 2014; Shew et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Decorrelated and sparse activity is a hallmark of adult spike trains.
source: Decorrelated and sparse activity is a hallmark of adult spike trains (Olshausen and Field, 2004; Vinje and Gallant, 2000) and artificial neural networks alike (Cun et al., 1990; Frankle and Carbin, 2019; Cogswell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Decorrelated and sparse activity is a hallmark of artificial neural networks.
source: Decorrelated and sparse activity is a hallmark of adult spike trains (Olshausen and Field, 2004; Vinje and Gallant, 2000) and artificial neural networks alike (Cun et al., 1990; Frankle and Carbin, 2019; Cogswell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Decorrelated and sparse activity allows for efficient storing and retrieval of information, while minimizing energy consumption.
source: This activity pattern bears important functional and behavioral relevance, as it allows for efficient storing and retrieval of information, while minimizing energy consumption (Olshausen and Field, 2004; Cun et al., 1990; Frankle and Carbin, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is unknown whether changes in E-I ratio underlie the developmental decorrelation of brain activity.
source: However, it is still unknown whether changes in E-I ratio underlie the developmental decorrelation of brain activity.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Altered E-I ratio is the hallmark of neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.
source: The (patho)physiological relevance of this process is underscored by the hypothesis that altered E-I ratio is the hallmark of later-emerging neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Antoine et al., 2019; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Gao and Penzes, 2015; Medendorp et al., 2021) and schizophrenia (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Ferguson and Gao, 2018), diseases that have also been linked to disruption of correlated activity in animal models (Luongo et al., 2016; Hamm et al., 2017; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Altered E-I ratio is the hallmark of neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia.
source: The (patho)physiological relevance of this process is underscored by the hypothesis that altered E-I ratio is the hallmark of later-emerging neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Antoine et al., 2019; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Gao and Penzes, 2015; Medendorp et al., 2021) and schizophrenia (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Ferguson and Gao, 2018), diseases that have also been linked to disruption of correlated activity in animal models (Luongo et al., 2016; Hamm et al., 2017; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Autism and schizophrenia have been linked to disruption of correlated activity in animal models.
source: The (patho)physiological relevance of this process is underscored by the hypothesis that altered E-I ratio is the hallmark of later-emerging neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Antoine et al., 2019; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Gao and Penzes, 2015; Medendorp et al., 2021) and schizophrenia (Gao and Penzes, 2015; Ferguson and Gao, 2018), diseases that have also been linked to disruption of correlated activity in animal models (Luongo et al., 2016; Hamm et al., 2017; Zick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Throughout development, both pyramidal neurons (PYRs) and interneurons (INs) migrate into the cortex following an 'inside-out' sequence that corresponds to their birthdate.
source: Throughout development, both populations of neurons migrate into the cortex following an 'inside-out' sequence that corresponds to their birthdate (Lim et al., 2018; Sidman and Rakic, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The migration process of neurons into the cortex is guided by cues provided by PYRs, which populate the cortical layers at an earlier time point than INs.
source: This process is guided by cues provided by PYRs, which populate the cortical layers at an earlier time point than INs (Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The functional integration of INs into the cortical circuitry is a slow process that is initiated by the establishment of transient circuits.
source: The functional integration of INs into the cortical circuitry is a slow process that is initiated by the establishment of transient circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: During the first postnatal week, mouse inhibitory circuits are dominated by somatostatin-positive (SST+) INs.
source: During the first postnatal week, mouse inhibitory circuits are dominated by somatostatin-positive (SST+) INs (Tuncdemir et al., 2016; Marques-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At later time points, parvalbumin-positive (PV+) INs are integrated into local networks.
source: At later time points, parvalbumin-positive (PV+) INs are also integrated into local networks (Tuncdemir et al., 2016; Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Guan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In rodents, the development of inhibitory synapses is not complete until postnatal day (P)30.
source: In rodents, the development of inhibitory synapses is not complete until postnatal day (P)30 (Gour et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The developmental strengthening of inhibitory synapses and the ensuing tilting of E-I ratio toward inhibition might underlie the decorrelation of neural activity.
source: It is thus conceivable that the developmental strengthening of inhibitory synapses and the ensuing tilting of E-I ratio toward inhibition (Zhang et al., 2011) might underlie the decorrelation of neural activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on previous findings.

claim: Chronic manipulation of IN activity in the murine barrel cortex results in altered temporal and spatial structure of brain activity.
source: In favor of this hypothesis, chronic manipulation of IN activity in the murine barrel cortex results in altered temporal and spatial structure of brain activity (Che et al., 2018; Duan et al., 2018; Modol et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct evidence linking E-I ratio and the strengthening of inhibition with the developmental decorrelation of brain activity is still lacking.
source: However, direct evidence linking E-I ratio and the strengthening of inhibition with the developmental decorrelation of brain activity is still lacking.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: It is debated whether GABA exerts an inhibitory effect during early development.
source: Further, it is still debated whether GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the adult brain, actually exerts an inhibitory effect also during early development.
evidence: This identifies a controversy in the field.

claim: In the rodent neocortex, GABA might act as an excitatory neurotransmitter for the first 2 postnatal weeks, and only subsequently 'switch' to an inhibitory effect.
source: It has long been thought that, in the rodent neocortex, GABA might act as an excitatory neurotransmitter for the first 2 postnatal weeks, and only subsequently 'switch' to an inhibitory effect (Ben-Ari, 2002; Kalemaki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work that is being questioned.

claim: The hypothesis that GABA acts as an excitatory neurotransmitter in early development has been called into question.
source: These findings have been called into question (Che et al., 2018; Kirmse et al., 2015; Murata and Colonnese, 2020), but the argument remains open.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work that challenges the earlier hypothesis.

claim: The proportion of active periods in the mPFC monotonically increases over age from P2 to P12.
source: To quantify this transition, we calculated the proportion of active periods over the recording and found that it monotonically increases over age (age slope = 0.88, 95% CI [0.84; 0.93], p<10–50, generalized linear model)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The maximum amplitude of active periods exponentially increases over age in the mPFC.
source: Accompanying these high-level changes in activity dynamics, the maximum amplitude of active periods, the broadband LFP power, and the SUA firing rate exponentially increased over age (age slope = 0.24, 0.47, and 0.21, 95% CI [0.18; 0.30], [0.40; 0.53], and [0.15; 0.27], p<10–9, p<10–23, p<10–11, respectively, generalized linear model)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The broadband LFP power exponentially increases over age in the mPFC.
source: Accompanying these high-level changes in activity dynamics, the maximum amplitude of active periods, the broadband LFP power, and the SUA firing rate exponentially increased over age (age slope = 0.24, 0.47, and 0.21, 95% CI [0.18; 0.30], [0.40; 0.53], and [0.15; 0.27], p<10–9, p<10–23, p<10–11, respectively, generalized linear model)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The SUA firing rate exponentially increases over age in the mPFC.
source: Accompanying these high-level changes in activity dynamics, the maximum amplitude of active periods, the broadband LFP power, and the SUA firing rate exponentially increased over age (age slope = 0.24, 0.47, and 0.21, 95% CI [0.18; 0.30], [0.40; 0.53], and [0.15; 0.27], p<10–9, p<10–23, p<10–11, respectively, generalized linear model)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: Changes in the log-log power spectral density (PSD) slope have been linked to E-I ratio by experimental studies.
source: Changes in the log-log power spectral density (PSD) slope (reflected by the 1/f exponent) have been linked to E-I ratio by several experimental (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Lendner et al., 2020; Colombo et al., 2019) and theoretical studies (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Lombardi et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Changes in the log-log power spectral density (PSD) slope have been linked to E-I ratio by theoretical studies.
source: Changes in the log-log power spectral density (PSD) slope (reflected by the 1/f exponent) have been linked to E-I ratio by several experimental (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Lendner et al., 2020; Colombo et al., 2019) and theoretical studies (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Lombardi et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A relative increase in inhibition leads to a steeper PSD slope (higher 1/f exponent).
source: In particular, a relative increase in inhibition is thought of leading to a steeper PSD slope (higher 1/f exponent), whereas the opposite occurs when E-I ratio shifts toward excitation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work.

claim: A shift of E-I ratio toward excitation leads to a less steep PSD slope (lower 1/f exponent).
source: In particular, a relative increase in inhibition is thought of leading to a steeper PSD slope (higher 1/f exponent), whereas the opposite occurs when E-I ratio shifts toward excitation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work.

claim: The PSD slope in the mPFC grows steeper over age from P2 to P12.
source: In line with this hypothesis, the PSD slope grew steeper over age, as readily observed when the PSD was normalized by the area under the curve (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The 1/f exponent in the mPFC increases with age from P2 to P12.
source: To quantify this observation, we parameterized the PSDs using a recently published protocol (Donoghue et al., 2020), and confirmed that the 1/f exponent increases with age (age slope = 0.12, 95% CI [0.11; 0.14], p<10–27, linear model) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the neural network model, increased net inhibition strength leads to an increase of the PSD 1/f exponent.
source: In agreement with previous results (Trakoshis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2017), the increase in the network's net inhibition strength robustly tilted the PSD slope (in the range from 30 to 100 Hz). Increased levels of net inhibition were associated with a steeper decay of power as a function of frequency and a corresponding increase of the 1/f exponent, across a range of AMPA conductance levels (Figure 2B); Pearson correlation coefficient, averaged across AMPA levels (inhibition strength slope = 0.022, 95% CI [0.021; 0.024], linear model).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the neural network model, increased net inhibition strength results in a logarithmic decrease in STTC.
source: For all levels of AMPA conductance, we found that increased net inhibition strength results in a robust logarithmic decrease in STTC (Figure 2C; inhibition strength slope = −0.068, 95% CI [0.075; 0.061], generalized linear model).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: STTC negatively correlates with the distance between neurons over all investigated lags.
source: Using multivariate mixed hierarchical linear regression, we found that STTC negatively correlated with the distance between neurons (i.e. nearby neurons had higher STTC values than neurons that are far apart) over all the investigated lags (main distance effect, p<10–78 at 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Nearby neurons have higher STTC values than neurons that are far apart.
source: Using multivariate mixed hierarchical linear regression, we found that STTC negatively correlated with the distance between neurons (i.e. nearby neurons had higher STTC values than neurons that are far apart) over all the investigated lags (main distance effect, p<10–78 at 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: STTC values negatively correlate with age at lags ≤5 s.
source: Further, STTC values negatively correlated with age at lags ≤5 s (main age effect, p<10–4 at 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model), an effect that was strongest in the 100–1000 ms range (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claim: The developmental STTC decrease does not occur uniformly across all neuron pairs.
source: This developmental STTC decrease did not occur uniformly across all neuron pairs.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Nearby pairs of neurons display a more severe decorrelation over age than neurons that are further apart.
source: Rather, age and distance had a significant interaction, nearby pairs of neurons displaying a more severe decorrelation over age than neurons that were further apart (age*distance interaction, p<10–12 at 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical support, shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of INs results in widespread inhibition of putative PYRs.
source: While putative INs increased their firing rate in response to optogenetic stimulation, a larger proportion of neurons (putative PYRs) significantly decreased their firing rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proportion of inhibited neurons increases with age during optogenetic IN stimulation.
source: In line with the results above that indicated increasing inhibition throughout development, the proportion of inhibited neurons augmented with age (main age effect = 0.31, 95% CI [0.09; 0.55], p=0.005, generalized linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 4C; individual dots correspond to optogenetic stimulation protocols, see figure legend and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: After terminating the optogenetic stimulus, PYRs respond with a prominent 'rebound' increase in firing rate.
source: Regardless of age, after terminating the optogenetic stimulus, PYRs responded with a prominent 'rebound' increase in firing rate, similar to the effects reported for the adult brain (Roux et al., 2014; Sessolo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments, with citations to similar findings in adult brain.

claim: GABA exerts an inhibitory population-level effect already during the first postnatal days.
source: Such widespread inhibition upon IN stimulation supports the hypothesis that GABA exerts an inhibitory population-level effect already during the first postnatal days.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The dynamics with which the PYR-IN network responds to IN activation does not change across the first 2 postnatal weeks.
source: These data indicate that, while the inhibition strength exerted by INs increases throughout development, the dynamics with which the PYR-IN network responds to IN activation does not change across the first 2 postnatal weeks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments and modeling.

claim: In the mPFC, GABA has an inhibitory role already at P2.
source: Thus, while the effects of GABA might differ within brain regions (Murata and Colonnese, 2020), our data supports the notion that, in the mPFC, GABA has an inhibitory role already at P2 and that even in the first postnatal days, the cortex operates in an ISN regime.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments and modeling.

claim: Even in the first postnatal days, the cortex operates in an ISN regime.
source: Thus, while the effects of GABA might differ within brain regions (Murata and Colonnese, 2020), our data supports the notion that, in the mPFC, GABA has an inhibitory role already at P2 and that even in the first postnatal days, the cortex operates in an ISN regime.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments and modeling.

claim: Light-induced IN silencing results in a widespread progressive increase of firing.
source: Light-induced IN silencing resulted in a widespread progressive increase of firing, with very few inhibited neurons (12/1611 neurons) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The proportion of neurons responding with a firing rate increase during IN inhibition increases with age.
source: The proportion of neurons responding with a firing rate increase during IN inhibition augmented with age (main age effect = 0.54, 95% CI [0.37; 0.74], p<10–8, generalized linear model) (Figure 5C; individual dots correspond to optogenetic stimulation protocols, see figure legend and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Putative INs have a biphasic response to optogenetic inhibition, initially being inhibited but then displaying a steep increase in firing rate.
source: On the contrary, and in line with previous experimental (Moore et al., 2018; Tsodyks et al., 1997; Sadeh and Clopath, 2020) and theoretical work (Kato et al., 2017; Sanzeni et al., 2020) in the adult brain, putative INs (the trajectory captured by the second component), had a biphasic response. They were initially inhibited but, halfway through the optogenetic stimulation, displayed a steep increase in firing rate, that persisted until end of the stimulus (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments, shown in Figure 5D, with citations to similar findings in adult brain.

claim: The biphasic response pattern of INs to inhibition is typical for inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs).
source: This response pattern is typical for inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs), a regime at which adult cortical circuits operate (Sanzeni et al., 2020; Sadeh et al., 2017), and that has been suggested to not characterize the early developing brain (Rahmati et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous work.

claim: Optogenetic IN stimulation results in decreased STTC values.
source: IN stimulation resulted in decreased STTC values (main IN stimulation effect, p<10–71, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Optogenetic IN inhibition increases STTC.
source: On the other hand, IN inhibition increased STTC (main IN inhibition effect, p<10–286, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: IN modulation has a larger impact on STTC values of nearby neurons when compared to pairs that are further apart.
source: Moreover, in line with the strongest decorrelation along development for nearby neurons (Figure 3D), IN modulation had a larger impact on STTC values of nearby neurons when compared to pairs that are further apart (IN stimulation*distance interaction, p=2*10–4; IN inhibition*distance interaction p<10–5, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments with statistical support, shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: GE mice have reduced excitatory activity in the superficial layers of the mPFC.
source: GE mice mimic the etiology (combined disruption of Disc1 gene and maternal immune activation) and cognitive impairment of schizophrenia, showing already at neonatal age reduced excitatory activity in the superficial layers of the mPFC (Chini et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on previously published data, with citations.

claim: Deep layers of the mPFC are not affected in GE mice.
source: On the flipside, deep layers of the mPFC are not affected.
evidence: This is stated based on previously published data.

claim: GE mice have lower STTC values than controls.
source: Overall, GE mice had lower spike train correlations when compared to controls (main condition effect, p=0.032, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claim: The STTC deficit in GE mice depends on whether the neuron pair is situated in the superficial or deep layers of the mPFC.
source: In line with the proposed hypothesis, this deficit depended on whether the neuron pair was situated in the superficial or deep layers of the mPFC (condition*layer interaction, p<10–7, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claim: There is no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers.
source: While there was no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers (p=0.15, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model), spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons was located in the superficial layers had reduced STTC values (p=0.016, 1 s lag).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claim: Spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons is located in the superficial layers have reduced STTC values.
source: While there was no significant difference between STTC of controls and GE spike train pairs situated in the deep layers (p=0.15, 1 s lag, linear mixed-effect model), spike train pairs of GE mice in which one of the two neurons was located in the superficial layers had reduced STTC values (p=0.016, 1 s lag).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support.

claim: The STTC difference is more robust if both neurons are situated in the superficial layers in GE mice.
source: This difference was even more robust if both neurons were situated in the superficial layers (p=10–3, 1 s lag) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of the GE mouse data with statistical support, shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: The 1/f exponent increases with age in newborn babies between 36 and 45 post-conception weeks.
source: We quantified the 1/f exponent on the 1–20 Hz frequency range and confirmed that it increased with age (age coefficient = 0.26, 95% CI [0.24; 0.27], p<10–183, linear model) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The 1/f exponent increases with age in babies recorded at 40 and 43 PCW.
source: The analyses revealed that also for these data the PSD slope grew steeper (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-C) and the 1/f exponent increased with age (age coefficient = 0.30, 95% CI [0.17; 0.42], p<10–4, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The increase in 1/f slope over age is similar across two different human EEG datasets.
source: The increase in 1/f slope over age was very similar across the two different datasets (mean age coefficients = 0.26 and 0.30) and no statistical difference was found between them (main dataset effect, p=0.15; age*dataset interaction, p=0.21, linear mixed-effect model) (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of human EEG data with statistical support, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The E-I ratio decreases along development in newborn humans.
source: Thus, the E-I ratio decreases along development also in newborn humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the human EEG data analysis.

claim: The developmental decrease in E-I ratio might represent a fingerprint of cortical circuit maturation in mammalian species.
source: This feature might represent a fingerprint of cortical circuit maturation in mammalian species.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings in both mice and humans.
